## AGI Basics

AGI describes a system that can learn or perform any intellectual task that a human can. The term has been used inconsistently for decades. Researchers disagree on whether benchmark scores are sufficient or whether embodiment is required. The debate goes back to the earliest days of the field and has not been fully resolved satisfactorily by anyone in the research community.

## Why the definition is contested

Some researchers argue that AGI requires consciousness or subjective experience, and that no purely computational system can exhibit those properties. Others take a functionalist view: if the system behaves indistinguishably from a general reasoner across a wide enough range of tasks, the internal substrate does not matter. The functionalist camp has tended to dominate in recent years as large language models have demonstrated surprisingly broad transfer across domains that were previously considered separate.

The benchmark approach to defining AGI has the advantage of being falsifiable. You set a threshold, you measure whether the model crosses it, and you have a verifiable answer. The disadvantage is that benchmarks saturate. When a benchmark is first published, state-of-the-art models fail it convincingly. Two or three model generations later, the scores are so high that the benchmark no longer discriminates well. At that point, researchers either retire the benchmark or argue that crossing it was never sufficient evidence of general capability in the first place.

## The role of transfer learning

Transfer learning is the ability of a model to apply knowledge gained in one domain to a different domain without task-specific retraining. It is arguably the most important capability that distinguishes narrow tools from genuinely general systems. A model that can read legal briefs and also diagnose dermatological conditions from photographs is demonstrating transfer across very different input distributions and reasoning styles.

Current models show impressive transfer across language-heavy domains. They struggle more with tasks that require physical intuition, spatial reasoning, or causal modeling based on intervention. These gaps are not mysterious: they reflect the training distribution. Models trained primarily on text will develop strong priors for text-like reasoning and weaker priors for embodied tasks. Closing the gap likely requires richer training data, better architectures, or both approaches pursued simultaneously.

## Long-horizon planning

Another capability used as a proxy for general intelligence is long-horizon planning: the ability to pursue a goal over many steps, adapting to new information as it arrives. This is distinct from single-shot reasoning, where the model sees a problem and produces an answer in one forward pass.

Long-horizon planning is harder to evaluate because it requires running the model in a loop, tracking its actions, and verifying whether its final state matches the intended goal. Several research groups have released agent evaluation frameworks that attempt to do this rigorously. The results show that models capable of impressive single-step reasoning often struggle to maintain coherent goals over dozens or hundreds of steps. Errors accumulate, context windows fill up, and the model loses track of earlier commitments made at the start of the task.

## Practical implications for builders

Product engineers should understand that the AGI debate, while philosophically interesting, is largely separate from the practical question of what models are useful for today. The useful question is not whether a model qualifies as AGI but whether it performs reliably on your specific tasks at an acceptable error rate and latency.

Designing for graceful degradation is essential. Every model has failure modes, and those failure modes will be triggered by real users doing real tasks in production. Building systems that handle model errors explicitly by flagging low-confidence outputs, asking for human review, or failing safely is more important than chasing the highest benchmark score.

The second dimension worth considering is the evaluation infrastructure problem. Running rigorous evaluations of long-horizon behavior is expensive and time-consuming. Most organizations simply do not invest in the tooling required to do it well, which means the failure rates are systematically underreported in industry benchmarks and public leaderboards alike. You need specialized environments, careful task specification, and human evaluators who can judge whether the model actually achieved the goal versus claiming to have done so. Most teams skip this work because their products do not yet depend on long-horizon reliability. That is a reasonable short-term trade-off, but it stores up technical debt: when you do need reliability over long horizons, you will have no baseline data to compare against.
